item.title: usb-rea generates a Linux driver for your Windows-only USB gadget
item.dc:creator: Jean-Luc Aufranc (CNXSoft)
item.description:
usb-rea is an MIT-licensed tool for people who own a USB gadget that only ships with a Windows program. It captures packets while you use the Windows app and generates a pyusb driver for Linux. Many years ago, I had to reverse-engineer a USB video capture card, whose vendor didn’t want to work with a company specializing in “small-volume production”. I had to capture the packets with Wireshark and manually implement code to replay URB (USB Request Block) packets using libusb, while paying close attention to timings. A tool like usb-rea would have been useful at the time. More specifically, usb-rea captures USB traffic with USBPcap or usbmon while the user clicks through the vendor app and labels the actions. The open-source program then infers the command structure (constants, counters, value fields, lookup tables, CRCs) and writes a Markdown protocol report plus a standalone Linux driver. The developer, Emir Mrkaljevic, [...]

item.title: Pinscope – A web-based remote access and vulnerability tracking solution for ESP32, Zephyr, Pico 2 W, and Linux SBCs
item.dc:creator: Jean-Luc Aufranc (CNXSoft)
item.description:
Pinscope is a remote-access service for microcontroller-class devices like ESP32, ESP8266, Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W, and other MCUs running Zephyr, as well as Raspberry Pi/Linux single board computers. The web-based solution features live logs, metrics, and crash reports, supports OTA updates that stop and roll back in case of failure, and tracks CRA security vulnerabilities for all supported platforms. Pinscope highlights: Web UI – The HTTP server already running on the device gets an HTTPS address of its own. Pages, APIs, and WebSockets work unchanged, behind the user’s login, a share link, or an API token. No port forwarding, no VPN needed. Health reporting – Heap, WiFi signal, chip temperature, restarts by reason, and the free stack of every task are reported with no code. Custom metrics can be added with one call. Logs  – ESP_LOG, Zephyr’s LOG_*, printf, etc. are stored.  Jump to a date and time or [...]

item.title: ST VL53LB is the smallest FlightSense ToF ranging sensor at just 4.0 × 1.8 × 1.0 mm
item.dc:creator: Jean-Luc Aufranc (CNXSoft)
item.description:
STMicroelectronics has just introduced the VL53LB (VL53LBCA), its smallest Time-of-Flight (ToF) ranging sensor, part of the FlightSense portfolio, with a size of just 4.0 × 1.8 × 1.0 mm. Like the earlier VL53L0X and VL53L1X models, it’s a single-zone ToF sensor featuring a 940 nm invisible vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser (VCSEL), but it offers a longer range of up to 8 meters and supports multi-object detection. It’s 30% smaller than the previous generation (VL53L3) and consumes just 50 µW in ULP mode, which makes it ideal for smartphones and space-constrained robotics and industrial systems. item.title: TinyWifiDongle Arduino library turns ESP32-S3 and Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W boards into USB WiFi adapters
item.dc:creator: Debashis Das
item.description:
TinyWifiDongle open-source Arduino library turns ESP32-S2/S3 and Raspberry Pi Pico W/2 W boards into USB WiFi adapters. The library uses USB CDC-NCM (Network Control Model) to provide network connectivity to Linux, macOS, and Windows 11 computers without installing additional drivers. The library implements a transparent Layer-2 bridge between the MCU’s WiFi and USB interfaces, allowing the connected computer to get an IP address directly from the router via DHCP, without NAT or a separate network. It supports hard-coded WiFi credentials or browser-based configuration and achieves approximately 5 Mbps on the ESP32-S3 and 2 Mbps on the Pico 2 W in the developer’s tests. TinyWifiDongle overview: Supported hardware ESP32-S3 and ESP32-S2 with native USB-OTG support; tested on ESP32-S3 Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W (RP2350) and Pico W (RP2040); tested on Pico 2 W ESP32-P4 (+ESP32-C6) support is experimental, with USB networking not yet tested USB networking – USB CDC-NCM using TinyUSB [...]

item.title: Tessera open-source dashboard for Home Assistant runs on ESP32 touchscreen devkits
item.dc:creator: Jean-Luc Aufranc (CNXSoft)
item.description:
The open-source Tessera project enables neat dashboards for Home Assistant on affordable 2.8-inch to 10.1-inch ESP32 touchscreen (development) kits from CYD, Guition, and Waveshare. The Tessera firmware adds a layer to ESPHome firmware for display management, touchscreen handling, dashboard rendering, tiles, plugins, and more. It works in conjunction with the Tessera Screen Manager, which provides the Home Assistant interface to configure screens, manage layouts, install firmware, and push updates. The whole solution is supposed to be easy to use thanks to a drag-and-drop editor, and users don’t need to know anything about YAML or MQTT. Tessera features highlights: Hardware support – Various ESP32 touchscreen platforms from 2.8-inch Cheap Yellow Displays (CYD) to 10.1-inch Guition panels. Drag-and-drop dashboard editor Configure screens, pages and tiles from Home Assistant. No YAML knowledge is needed. Multi-page dashboards – Organize controls across multiple pages Customizable layouts – Configure grid dimensions, tile sizes, icons, colours and [...]

item.title: Piccola CNC – An open-source hardware desktop milling machine with PCB auto-leveling and integrated CAM (Crowdfunding)
item.dc:creator: Debashis Das
item.description:
InMachines Ingrassia GmbH has launched the Piccola CNC, an open-source hardware desktop CNC milling machine designed for PCB prototyping and machining wood, plastics, and soft metals such as aluminum, brass, and copper. Built in Germany, the machine features a 150 × 150 × 70 mm work area, belt-driven ball screws on all three axes, ER11 collets, and a choice of 100W or 200W spindles. The machine comes in three versions, which include the Basic, Pro, and Ultimate. The Pro variant adds a full enclosure and safety interlocks, while the Ultimate model further adds a brushless spindle and laser distance sensor. Other features include USB-C and Wi-Fi connectivity, built-in CAM software for PCB, 2D, 3D, and rotary milling, and laser-based PCB height mapping on the Ultimate, with the sensor available as an accessory for Basic and Pro. item.title: AMD EPYC Embedded 9006 Series embedded processors offer up to 256 Zen 6c cores, PCIe Gen 6, and CXL 3.1
item.dc:creator: Debashis Das
item.description:
AMD has introduced the EPYC Embedded 9006 Series SP7, a family of high-performance x86 SoCs built around the Zen 6 and Zen 6c architectures using a 2nm CPU process. Designed for semiconductor automated test equipment (ATE), networking appliances, firewalls, and enterprise storage controllers, the new embedded processors feature up to 256 cores, 512 threads, and 1GB of L3 cache, with power ratings ranging from 400W to 600W. Compared to the previous-generation EPYC Embedded 9005 Series, the new processors offer 16-channel DDR5 memory with RDIMM and MRDIMM support, up to 96 PCIe Gen 6 lanes, and CXL 3.1 connectivity. They also offer improved security, enterprise-class reliability, and seven-year product availability, making them suitable for long-lifecycle embedded systems. item.title: Waveshare ESP32-S31-Touch-LCD-4.3C – An ESP32-S31 4.3-inch display devkit with optional DIN rail case
item.dc:creator: Jean-Luc Aufranc (CNXSoft)
item.description:
Last month we wrote about VIEWE’s ESP32-S31 4.3-inch touch display, but there’s now another option, namely the Waveshare ESP32-S31-Touch-LCD-4.3C development kit. Both models are similar, with an ESP32-S31 module equipped with 16MB flash and 16MB PSRAM, a 4.3-inch 800×480  touchscreen display, RS485 and CAN Bus interfaces, and more. The EVIEW model supports 16.7M colors, while the Waveshare devkit is limited to 65K colors, but it offers a wider 7V-36V voltage input, an optional DIN rail enclosure, and 3.7V Lithium battery support. item.title: Bluetooth 7.0 specification ratified with HDT (High Data Throughput) support
item.dc:creator: Jean-Luc Aufranc (CNXSoft)
item.description:
The Bluetooth SIG ratified the Bluetooth 7.0 specification on November 3, 2026, with the highlight of the new Bluetooth Core specification being optional support for HDT (High Data Throughput), delivering up to 7.5 Mbps bitrate. We first covered HDT in 2025 when initial/early support was implemented into the Ceva-Waves Links200 multi-protocol platform IP, and followed last September with the Realtek RTL8773J Bluetooth 7-ready Cortex-M55/M33 microcontroller. The main news is that the specification for Bluetooth 7.0 and the associated HDT feature is officially ratified/adopted. Bluetooth 7.0 highlights: Bluetooth High Data Throughput (HDT) introduces a new Bluetooth LE physical layer that increases the maximum Bluetooth bit rate to 7.5 Mbps while improving wireless efficiency and robustness. The higher bitrate is enabled by a combination of higher-order modulation, convolutional forward error correction, synchronization enhancements, adaptive rate selection, and enhanced packet architectures. It will be especially useful for high-resolution and lossless audio streaming. Bluetooth [...]

item.title: Web-based breadboard simulator lets you build circuits, fix errors, and monitor designs with a built-in oscilloscope
item.dc:creator: Jean-Luc Aufranc (CNXSoft)
item.description:
Dev Kapadia’s de:volt is a breadboard simulator that runs in your browser. You can place parts and wires on a breadboard, and the circuit runs live the whole time as you build it. The project aims to be as close as a real breadboard would be. It reports errors and warnings, and you can monitor pins with its built-in oscilloscope and/or multimeter. For instance, an LED with no resistor burns out, a weak battery sags under load, a motor pulls current, and a 555 on the 4-channel scope shows its timing capacitor charging and discharging. de:volt highlights: Build circuits on a virtual breadboard using the 105 parts available from the interface: resistors, capacitors, diodes, transistors, LEDs, 555 timers, 74-series and CD4000 logic, EEPROMs, motor drivers, sensors, and more. Four Arduino, BBC micro:bit, and RP2040 MCU boards are also available, and you can write and run MicroPython code from the web [...]

item.title: 750 MHz GigaDevice GD32H7 Cortex-M7 MCU family gets up to 9.5MB Flash, EtherCAT for industrial applications
item.dc:creator: Debashis Das
item.description:
GigaDevice adds new industrial parts to the GD32H7 series of Cortex-M7 MCUs, running at up to 750 MHz. The new lineup includes the GD32H77R for robotic joint control, GD32H78D/77D for industrial HMI applications, GD32H78E/77E for real-time motion control, and GD32H789/779 for general industrial automation. The MCUs feature up to 9728KB of on-chip Flash, 1152KB SRAM including 640KB tightly coupled memory (TCM), and hardware accelerators for mathematical operations and digital signal processing. Depending on the variant, they also integrate a MIPI DSI display interface, an EtherCAT slave controller, industrial encoder interfaces, dual Ethernet, and three CAN-FD controllers. The devices target servo drives, humanoid robots, industrial displays, CNC machines, PLCs, and digital power systems.
